prompt:
Write an opinion piece of about 800 words on whether cities should remove minimum parking requirements from their planning rules. Take a side and argue for it.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Let the length of each sentence follow what it has to say. Do not use a short sentence to set up a longer one.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.

text:
Cities should remove their minimum parking requirements, and they should do it soon, because the rules ask planners to predict something no planner can know and then bind every builder to the guess. A parking minimum says that a restaurant must provide so many spaces per hundred square feet of dining room, that an apartment building must supply one or two spaces per unit, that a small office must set aside a fixed share of its lot for cars. These numbers usually trace back to manuals that averaged out the peak demand observed at a handful of suburban sites, often places with free parking and no alternatives to driving, and then hardened into law as though they described what every neighborhood needs. Donald Shoup, whose book The High Cost of Free Parking made the case against them, found that the standards had little empirical footing and that cities copied one another's figures without checking whether they fit local conditions.

The first cost is paid in land and money, and it is paid whether or not anyone ever parks there. A surface space takes up roughly three hundred square feet once you include the aisle that lets a car reach it, and a structured or underground space can cost tens of thousands of dollars to build, which developers fold into rents and prices. A household that owns no car still pays for the parking attached to its apartment, because the building cannot legally exist without it. The requirement therefore works as a tax on housing that falls hardest on the people with the least money, who are also the people most likely to live without a car, and it hides inside the rent so that nobody sees the line item.

The second cost is the buildings that never get built. Many small lots in older neighborhoods cannot physically hold the required spaces alongside a viable building, so a corner store, a fourplex, or a conversion of an old warehouse into apartments simply fails to pencil out, and the lot stays vacant or underused. Cities that complain about housing shortages while mandating several hundred square feet of asphalt per home are working against themselves. When Buffalo eliminated its citywide minimums in 2017, and when Minneapolis and Seattle and a growing list of others followed in various forms, the point was partly to stop making this particular obstacle part of every proposal, and early evidence from places that have relaxed the rules suggests developers often build less parking than the old law demanded once they are free to choose, which tells you how much of the mandated supply was surplus.

The strongest objection is that without minimums, new buildings will spill their cars onto the surrounding streets and neighbors will pay the price in congestion and lost convenience. That worry deserves a serious answer, and the answer is that the problem lies with how the street is priced, not with whether a developer was forced to build spaces. Curb parking that is free and unmanaged will always fill up, with or without minimums, and the remedy is to charge for it at a level that keeps a space or two open on each block, with revenue returned to the neighborhood through a parking benefit district that pays for sidewalks, trees, and lighting. Residential permit programs can reserve curb space for people who live nearby. Removing a minimum does not forbid a building from including parking; it lets the builder, the lender, and the tenant decide how much is worth paying for, and lenders in particular remain wary of projects they think will struggle to attract tenants, so most suburban-style developments would keep generous parking regardless.

Another objection holds that people in many places still need cars, and that taking away the requirement punishes the disabled, the elderly, and families with children. But repeal does not take away anyone's car or parking space; it takes away the compulsion on the person building something new. Accessible spaces can and should stay mandatory under disability law, which is a different question from a blanket ratio of spaces to floor area. And places where driving really is necessary will keep supplying parking because their customers demand it, as every suburban shopping center that wants to stay full already understands. The rule only bites in the cases where the market would have chosen less, which are exactly the dense, walkable, transit-served places where a city has said it wants more people to live without needing to own a vehicle.

There is also a fairness argument that gets too little attention. Minimums force everyone to subsidize driving, including the household that bikes to work, the tenant who sold their car to afford rent, and the shopper who walks from three blocks away, since the cost of the spaces is spread across prices they pay anyway. Taking the mandate away lets that cost appear where it belongs, on the people who use the spaces, and it lets a business that attracts customers on foot spend its money on something other than a lot that sits empty at most hours of the week.

A city that wants to correct course does not need to ban parking or to pretend cars are going away. It can strike the numbers from the code, keep accessibility requirements, price the curb sensibly, and let each project respond to the street it actually sits on. The result will be more housing on lots that were previously unusable, cheaper rents at the margin, more room for trees and storefronts and people, and rules that no longer rest on a guess made decades ago about a place that has changed since. Planning should set the conditions for a good city and then trust the people who build and live in it to work out how many parking spaces they need.
